solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing; clues and answers read from cryptics.georgeho.org (ODbL)'s copy of the post

clue.text: "Let your hair down", gals, in training for Mayday!

parts.note: read literally, to undo your tresses is to dis-tress, so the phrase gives the letters DISTRESS

indicators.note: in training, the letters are being drilled and put through new formations, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: An exclamation about girls letting their hair down during practice for May Day festivities.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Let your hair down' is read as dis-tress (unpick the tresses); 'training' rearranges GALS IN to make SIGNAL.
explanation.definitionFit: Mayday is the international radio call used by ships and aircraft in grave danger, a classic emergency call for help.

clue.text: Work surface of French finish placed round edge of kitchen

parts.note: de is French for of

indicators.note: the word for finish is placed around another piece, enclosing it

parts.note: to finish is to stop

indicators.note: the edge of a word is its opening letter, here the first of kitchen

explanation.surface: A kitchen worktop with a French-style finish fitted around its edge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'placed round' makes the word for finish wrap the kitchen's edge letter, giving SKTOP; 'French finish' reads as a varnish but splits into two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A desk's top is the flat surface you write and work at, and the word also names a computer screen's main work area.

clue.text: Lips to endlessly pucker and home to mostly discover it — I've just done this twice!

indicators.note: to pucker is to crumple or wrinkle, so these letters are crumpled into a new order
the word to loses its final letter, having no end

parts.note: in means at home

indicators.note: most of the word, all but its last letter

parts.note: to discover is to find
the contraction I've supplies the letters I, V, E

explanation.surface: An instruction to purse your lips and go home to find something, with the setter boasting of a grammatical crime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to endlessly pucker' and 'to mostly discover' each wedge an adverb between to and its verb, the very fault defined. 'pucker' rearranges the lips plus T into the first word.
explanation.definitionFit: Placing an adverb between to and the verb, as the setter has done twice in this clue, is the grammatical fault purists condemn.

clue.text: Ramble sounds capital

indicators.note: sounds signals that the capital city, said out loud, gives a word spelt differently

parts.note: Rome is the capital of Italy

explanation.surface: A short note that wandering around sounds like a great idea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sounds' looks like part of a verdict ('sounds capital' as in 'sounds splendid'), but it is the sound-alike signal; 'capital' is the city.
explanation.definitionFit: To ramble is to wander about without a fixed route, which is the same as to rove or wander freely.

clue.text: Drunk did away with education

parts.note: slew is the past tense of slay, to kill or do away with

explanation.surface: A tipsy person who abandoned schooling.
explanation.definitionFit: Slewed is informal slang for intoxicated, like tight or sloshed.

clue.text: Shocking us with extra pennies — many of them!

definitions.text: Shocking us with extra pennies — many of them!

indicators.note: shocking means jolting or disturbing, so the letters that follow are thrown into a new order

parts.note: p is the abbreviation for pence or pennies

explanation.surface: A complaint about an outrageous extra charge taking many pennies from us.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shocking' rearranges US, EXTRA and P; the whole clue then describes the answer, a levy that takes many extra pennies.
explanation.definitionFit: An extra levy charged on top of normal income tax for high earners takes a great deal more money, a shock to the payer.

clue.text: Guards ringleaders left out to fester

indicators.note: to fester is to rot or decay, so the remaining letters go bad and fall into a new order
out signals that the letter for left is removed from the word

explanation.surface: Soldiers on guard leave the ringleaders of a mutiny to rot in a cell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'left out' removes L from RINGLEADERS, leaving RINGEADERS, which 'to fester' rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: The Grenadier Guards are a regiment of the British Army's foot guards, so its soldiers are guards.

clue.text: In the morning, employ workers on "Sailor Jack" sideshow

parts.note: am stands for ante meridiem, the morning
to employ something is to use it
men can mean workers, as in management and men
tar is an old word for a sailor
Jack Cade led a rebellion against Henry VI in 1450

explanation.surface: A morning hire of staff to run a fairground sideshow called Sailor Jack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sailor Jack' looks like one name, the sideshow's, but splits in two: Jack Cade was the leader of a Kentish rebellion in 1450.
explanation.definitionFit: A hall full of slot machines and games is a seaside entertainment, loosely a sideshow alongside the main attractions.

clue.text: The Yorkshire bench

definitions.meaning: ... is a market town in North Yorkshire, at the start of the ... to Carlisle railway
a high-backed wooden bench seat, often with a chest beneath

explanation.surface: A seat made in or typical of Yorkshire.
explanation.walkthrough: Settle is a small town in the Yorkshire Dales, the northern English county; the clue reads as one piece of furniture.
explanation.definitionFit: A long wooden seat with a high back and arms is the traditional furniture piece, and the same name belongs to a Yorkshire town.

clue.text: Leaves with Group of Founders for the border

indicators.note: to founder is to collapse or sink, so the letters fall apart and are rebuilt

parts.note: G is an abbreviation for group, as in G7 or G20

explanation.surface: A company quits a group of founding members to go to the border.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Founders' looks like a noun naming the group, but it is a verb, the signal to rearrange LEAVES with G.
explanation.definitionFit: The selvage is the self-finished edge of woven fabric that stops it fraying, a border on the cloth.

clue.text: Overture from "The Puritan" enthralling the Spanish

indicators.note: enthralling means holding captive, so one piece holds the other inside it

parts.note: a puritan is a prude, someone easily shocked by impropriety
el is Spanish for the

explanation.surface: An opening piece of music taken from an opera called The Puritan, with Spanish performers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Puritan' looks like an opera title in quotes (Bellini wrote I Puritani) but is just a prim person; 'enthralling' holds the Spanish article inside.
explanation.definitionFit: An introductory musical piece played before the main work is both an overture and a prelude.

clue.text: Skirt Tuvalu's margins repeatedly

indicators.note: repeatedly says the pair of letters is written out twice in a row
the margins of a word are its two outside letters, the first and the last

explanation.surface: An instruction to skirt round the edges of the Pacific nation of Tuvalu again and again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Skirt' looks like a verb (go round the edge), matching 'margins', but it is the noun; 'margins' of TUVALU gives TU, doubled by 'repeatedly'.
explanation.definitionFit: A ballerina's short stiff skirt of layered net is the classic garment of classical ballet.

clue.text: Back Massachusetts workers to gain tons of new equipment

parts.note: the rear is the back
MA is the postal abbreviation for Massachusetts
men as workers, as in management and men

explanation.surface: Supporting American workers in Massachusetts as they acquire lots of new kit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back' looks like a verb (support), but it gives the noun REAR.
explanation.definitionFit: Arming again means supplying an army with fresh weapons and kit, so it is a refit with new military equipment.

clue.text: Fetch punt or lose your job!

definitions.meaning: fetch is get, and a punt is a kick from the hands, taken as the boot
to be dismissed from employment, idiomatically

explanation.surface: An employee told to retrieve a boat, or else be fired.
explanation.walkthrough: 'punt' suggests a boat (with 'Fetch' a boatyard order), but here it is a kick of a ball, as in rugby.
explanation.definitionFit: Being sacked from your work is idiomatically being kicked out, and literally to receive a kick is the same phrase.

clue.text: Boatman's customer

definitions.meaning: someone who propels a flat-bottomed boat with a pole, as on the Cam at Cambridge
in British slang, a client or customer, also someone who bets

explanation.surface: A boatman's client.
explanation.walkthrough: A punt is a flat boat pushed along with a pole on English rivers; British slang also uses the answer word for a customer or a gambler.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both one who poles a punt along a river and, informally, a paying customer or a bettor.

clue.text: With tear-gas enveloping Joe, you sound an alarm with this

indicators.note: enveloping means wrapping around, so the soldier sits inside the gas

parts.note: Mace is a brand of tear gas spray
GI Joe is a nickname for an American soldier, so Joe gives GI
ye is an old form of you

explanation.surface: Gassing an American soldier would surely set the alarms ringing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'enveloping' wraps the spray round the soldier; the definition describes what the device does rather than naming it.
explanation.definitionFit: A photoelectric cell that trips when a light beam is broken is a common trigger for a burglar alarm.

clue.text: Become exhausted with visit by daughter

parts.note: to visit someone is to go to see them
d is the abbreviation for daughter in family trees

explanation.surface: Someone worn out after a visit from their daughter.
explanation.definitionFit: A plant that bolts into flowering stops being productive, and figuratively a person or place gone to ruin is spent, run down.

clue.text: Bucket of "poison" thrown over abstainer

indicators.note: over says the scrambled word is placed all around the other piece
thrown suggests the letters are tossed about and land in a new order

parts.note: TT stands for teetotal, a person who abstains from alcohol

explanation.surface: A bucket of poison flung over a teetotaller.
explanation.walkthrough: 'thrown' rearranges the poison as SPIOON, and 'over' wraps it round the abstainer's letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A receptacle for spitting into, once common in bars, is a kind of bucket or bowl.

clue.text: Prophet united in corresponding with Levites' leader

indicators.note: in says the letter for united goes inside the word for corresponding

parts.note: corresponding things are the same
U is the abbreviation for united, as in football club names

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its opening letter

explanation.surface: A prophet in agreement with the head of the Levites, the priestly tribe of Israel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts U inside SAME, and 'Levites' leader' adds L.
explanation.definitionFit: The Old Testament prophet who anointed Saul and David as kings of Israel was Hannah's son, a major biblical seer.

clue.text: Support routine job in Catholic church

indicators.note: in says the routine is placed inside the letters for Catholic church

parts.note: a rut is a dull routine

explanation.surface: Backing a humdrum task in a Catholic church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' splits the Catholic and church abbreviations to hold the routine; 'Support' could be a verb, but the answer is the noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A prop placed under the arm to help a lame person walk is a support, and figuratively anything leaned on.

clue.text: Home partially in Panama?

indicators.note: in says one piece is placed inside the other

parts.note: a Panama is a straw hat
partially means to some degree, or a bit

explanation.surface: Asks whether home is partly in the Central American country of Panama.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Panama' looks like the country but is the straw hat; 'partially' gives A BIT, which 'in' puts inside HAT.
explanation.definitionFit: The natural environment where an animal or plant lives is its home ground.

clue.text: Boy's under water for a time

indicators.note: in a down answer, under means placed beneath, so it comes second

parts.note: the sea is a body of water
a son is a boy

explanation.surface: A boy swimming underwater for a while.
explanation.walkthrough: 'under' puts SON below SEA in the down answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A season is a period of the year, such as summer or the football season, so it is a stretch of time.

clue.text: I'm Ned, I am, making cheap deliveries

parts.note: write the word for a first or unmarried girl and then read it over, back to front, and it spells Ned, I am

explanation.surface: Ned introduces himself twice while bowling economically.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: MAIDEN turned over reads NEDIAM, 'Ned, I am'. In cricket an over is six balls; a maiden over concedes no runs, so its deliveries cost the fielding side nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket, six balls from which the batsman scores nothing have cost the bowler no runs, so they are cheap.

clue.text: Grey lady? Not her!

definitions.meaning: dull and colourless, of a dingy brownish-grey
an old word for a slattern or a woman of loose morals, the opposite of a lady

explanation.surface: Asks whether a grey lady is meant, and replies that she is not.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is archaic: a woman of low repute, hence the very opposite of a lady.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means dull and dingy in colour, and as an old noun it named a slovenly woman, no lady at all.

clue.text: Conduct uneven wrangle

indicators.note: uneven picks the odd-numbered letters, first, third, fifth and seventh

explanation.surface: A rude, ill-matched quarrel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Conduct' looks like a noun (behaviour) but is the verb, as in conduct a campaign.
explanation.definitionFit: To conduct a campaign or war is to carry it on, the sense found in waging war.

clue.text: Model gets warning shortly after drug depression

indicators.note: after says the shortened warning comes behind the other pieces

parts.note: E is slang for the drug ecstasy
a pit is a hollow or depression in the ground

indicators.note: shortly means cut short, losing the last letter

parts.note: an omen is a warning sign

explanation.surface: A fashion model gets a brief caution after a drug-induced low.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shortly' drops the warning's last letter, leaving OME, and 'after' puts it last; 'depression' looks like low mood but is a hole.
explanation.definitionFit: A perfect example or embodiment of a quality is a model of it.

clue.text: Boy camps in agreed pitch

indicators.note: to camp in somewhere is to settle inside it, so the boy sits within the other word

parts.note: set means settled or agreed, as in it's all set
Alan is a boy's name

explanation.surface: A lad pitches his tent on the agreed pitch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'camps in' settles the boy inside the word for agreed; 'pitch' looks like a campsite or playing field, but it is the tarry substance.
explanation.definitionFit: Pitch is a black tarry substance used to make joints and hulls watertight, a sealing material.

clue.text: Setter's evident bungling creates particular concern

indicators.note: bungling means messing up, so the letters are botched into a new order

parts.note: the possessive is taken as the plain letters of setter plus S

explanation.surface: The setter admits that clumsy work causes a specific worry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bungling' rearranges SETTERS EVIDENT, using the S of the possessive.
explanation.definitionFit: A personal stake that makes someone care about an outcome is a special interest, often a financial one.
